brief: TS Lombard's Blitz argues raising the funds rate and inverting the curve would be symbolic but ineffective, because private-sector debt is a shrinking share of total debt creation while Federal borrowing, insensitive to rate levels, keeps spending and inflation running. Since 2012 inflation tracks Federal debt growth (6-quarter lag) more than household/business debt (4-quarter lag), reversing the pre-2012 pattern. This makes yield-curve inversion slower to trigger recession; the last inversion (25 months) never produced one. Blitz's base case: Warsh uses the incoming CPI print to avoid a September hike and instead lets the curve steepen, a route he says Bessent and Warsh's task force are also considering: hold the funds rate, let Treasury borrow cheaply short-term, and let the market push 10-year yields up to match supply and demand. If Warsh hikes anyway, the usual buy-30s/sell-10s trade may not hold. Supporting evidence: households have not returned to pre-GFC credit-fueled retail spending, corporate balance sheets are less rate-sensitive, and the 10Y-forward-to-spot spread may not fall this time as it typically has after past hikes.
